claim: Around 38 million people worldwide are living with HIV.
source: Around 38 million people worldwide are living with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and every year, 1. 7million people get newly infected (UNALDS, 2020).
evidence: Cited from UNALDS, 2020 report

claim: Every year, 1.7 million people get newly infected with HIV.
source: Around 38 million people worldwide are living with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and every year, 1. 7million people get newly infected (UNALDS, 2020).
evidence: Cited from UNALDS, 2020 report

claim: Combined antiretroviral therapy (cART) can suppress viremia and dramatically improved the life expectancy and clinical outcome of HIV-1 infected patients.
source: Although combined antiretroviral therapy (cART) can suppress viremia and dramatically improved the life expectancy and the clinical outcome of HIV-1 infected patients (Antiretroviral Therapy Cohort Collaboration, 2008), optimal cART treatment is not curative due to the persistence of a lifelong HIV-1 replication competent reservoir (Siliciano et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from Antiretroviral Therapy Cohort Collaboration, 2008

claim: Optimal cART treatment is not curative due to the persistence of a lifelong HIV-1 replication competent reservoir.
source: Although combined antiretroviral therapy (cART) can suppress viremia and dramatically improved the life expectancy and the clinical outcome of HIV-1 infected patients (Antiretroviral Therapy Cohort Collaboration, 2008), optimal cART treatment is not curative due to the persistence of a lifelong HIV-1 replication competent reservoir (Siliciano et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from Siliciano et al., 2003

claim: cART does not fully resolve HIV-associated immune abnormalities including low-grade chronic inflammation, immune activation/dysfunction, and poor CD4+ T cell reconstitution.
source: In addition, cART does not fully resolve HIV-associated immune abnormalities including low-grade chronic inflammation, immune activation/dysfunction, and poor CD4+ T cell reconstitution (French et al., 2009; Hunt et al., 2003) and imposes a high burden to the health care system due to treatment resistance, adverse events, and high treatment costs.
evidence: Cited from French et al., 2009 and Hunt et al., 2003

claim: Inflammation drives HIV-1 reservoirs persistence which in turn contributes to inflammation, creating a pathogenic vicious cycle.
source: Recent evidence indicates that inflammation drives HIV-1 reservoirs persistence which in turn contributes to inflammation, creating a pathogenic vicious cycle (Klatt et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Klatt et al., 2013

claim: Inflammatory and immune disorders predispose HIV-1 infected patients under cART to non-AIDS age-related comorbid conditions such as cardiovascular diseases, cancer, and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: These inflammatory and immune disorders predispose HIV-1 infected patients under cART to non-AIDS age-related comorbid conditions such as cardiovascular diseases, cancer, and neurodegenerative diseases and are predictive of an increased risk of morbidity and mortality (Kuller et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from Kuller et al., 2008

claim: Expression of caspase-1, NLRP3, and IL-1β was increased in lymph nodes and bone marrow between day 1 and 3 after HIV-1 infection with mean fold changes of 2.08, 3.23, and 6.05 (p<0.001).
source: Expression of caspase-1, NLRP3, and IL-1β was increased in lymph nodes and bone marrow between day 1 and 3 after HIV-1 infection (mean fold change (FC) of 2.08, 3.23, and 6.05, p<0.001, respectively).
evidence: Experimental data from the study showing gene expression changes

claim: IFI16 and AIM2 expression peaked at day 24 post-infection.
source: IFI16 and AIM2 expression peaked at day 24 and coincides with increased IL-18 levels (6.89 vs 83.19 pg/ml, p=0.004), increased viral load and CD4+ T cells loss in blood (p<0.005 and p<0.0001, for the spleen respectively).
evidence: Experimental data from the study showing gene expression kinetics

claim: IL-18 levels increased from 6.89 to 83.19 pg/ml at day 24 (p=0.004).
source: IFI16 and AIM2 expression peaked at day 24 and coincides with increased IL-18 levels (6.89 vs 83.19 pg/ml, p=0.004), increased viral load and CD4+ T cells loss in blood (p<0.005 and p<0.0001, for the spleen respectively).
evidence: Experimental data from the study measuring cytokine levels

claim: Treatment with VX-765 significantly reduced TNF-α at day 11 (0.47 vs 2.2 pg/ml, p=0.045).
source: Treatment with VX-765 significantly reduced TNF-α at day 11 (0.47 vs 2.2 pg/ml, p=0.045), IL-18 at day 22 (7.8 vs 23.2 pg/ml, p=0.04), CD4+ T cells (44.3% vs 36,7%, p=0.01), viral load (4.26 vs 4.89 log 10 copies/ml, p=0.027), and total HIV-1 DNA in the spleen (1 054 vs 2 889 copies /106 cells, p=0.029).
evidence: Experimental data from VX-765 treatment study

claim: Treatment with VX-765 significantly reduced IL-18 at day 22 (7.8 vs 23.2 pg/ml, p=0.04).
source: Treatment with VX-765 significantly reduced TNF-α at day 11 (0.47 vs 2.2 pg/ml, p=0.045), IL-18 at day 22 (7.8 vs 23.2 pg/ml, p=0.04), CD4+ T cells (44.3% vs 36,7%, p=0.01), viral load (4.26 vs 4.89 log 10 copies/ml, p=0.027), and total HIV-1 DNA in the spleen (1 054 vs 2 889 copies /106 cells, p=0.029).
evidence: Experimental data from VX-765 treatment study

claim: Treatment with VX-765 significantly increased CD4+ T cells (44.3% vs 36.7%, p=0.01).
source: Treatment with VX-765 significantly reduced TNF-α at day 11 (0.47 vs 2.2 pg/ml, p=0.045), IL-18 at day 22 (7.8 vs 23.2 pg/ml, p=0.04), CD4+ T cells (44.3% vs 36,7%, p=0.01), viral load (4.26 vs 4.89 log 10 copies/ml, p=0.027), and total HIV-1 DNA in the spleen (1 054 vs 2 889 copies /106 cells, p=0.029).
evidence: Experimental data from VX-765 treatment study

source: Treatment with VX-765 significantly reduced TNF-α at day 11 (0.47 vs 2.2 pg/ml, p=0.045), IL-18 at day 22 (7.8 vs 23.2 pg/ml, p=0.04), CD4+ T cells (44.3% vs 36,7%, p=0.01), viral load (4.26 vs 4.89 log 10 copies/ml, p=0.027), and total HIV-1 DNA in the spleen (1 054 vs 2 889 copies /106 cells, p=0.029).
evidence: Experimental data from VX-765 treatment study

claim: Treatment with VX-765 significantly reduced total HIV-1 DNA in the spleen (1,054 vs 2,889 copies/10^6 cells, p=0.029).
source: Treatment with VX-765 significantly reduced TNF-α at day 11 (0.47 vs 2.2 pg/ml, p=0.045), IL-18 at day 22 (7.8 vs 23.2 pg/ml, p=0.04), CD4+ T cells (44.3% vs 36,7%, p=0.01), viral load (4.26 vs 4.89 log 10 copies/ml, p=0.027), and total HIV-1 DNA in the spleen (1 054 vs 2 889 copies /106 cells, p=0.029).
evidence: Experimental data from VX-765 treatment study

claim: Targeting inflammasome activation early after infection may represent a therapeutic strategy towards HIV cure to prevent CD4+ T cell depletion and reduce immune activation, viral load, and the HIV-1 reservoir formation.
source: We demonstrated that targeting inflammasome activation early after infection may represent a therapeutic strategy towards HIV cure to prevent CD4+ T cell depletion and reduce immune activation, viral load, and the HIV-1 reservoir formation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data showing effects of VX-765 treatment

claim: HIV infection triggers immune activation/dysfunction and inflammation through direct effects of viral proteins on immune cells.
source: HIV infection triggers immune activation/dysfunction and inflammation through several mechanisms such as direct effects of viral proteins on immune cells (Rieckmann et al., 1991; Lee et al., 2003; Simmons et al., 2001), persistent production of type I and II interferons driven by activation of toll-like receptors with HIV-1 RNA (Sereti and Altfeld, 2016), fibrosis of lymphoid structure linked to CD4+ T cells depletion (Beignon et al., 2005) and mucosal barriers damages associated with microbial translocation (Klatt and Brenchley, 2010; Gordon et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from Rieckmann et al., 1991; Lee et al., 2003; Simmons et al., 2001

claim: HIV infection triggers immune activation/dysfunction and inflammation through persistent production of type I and II interferons driven by activation of toll-like receptors with HIV-1 RNA.
source: HIV infection triggers immune activation/dysfunction and inflammation through several mechanisms such as direct effects of viral proteins on immune cells (Rieckmann et al., 1991; Lee et al., 2003; Simmons et al., 2001), persistent production of type I and II interferons driven by activation of toll-like receptors with HIV-1 RNA (Sereti and Altfeld, 2016), fibrosis of lymphoid structure linked to CD4+ T cells depletion (Beignon et al., 2005) and mucosal barriers damages associated with microbial translocation (Klatt and Brenchley, 2010; Gordon et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from Sereti and Altfeld, 2016

claim: HIV infection triggers immune activation/dysfunction and inflammation through fibrosis of lymphoid structure linked to CD4+ T cells depletion.
source: HIV infection triggers immune activation/dysfunction and inflammation through several mechanisms such as direct effects of viral proteins on immune cells (Rieckmann et al., 1991; Lee et al., 2003; Simmons et al., 2001), persistent production of type I and II interferons driven by activation of toll-like receptors with HIV-1 RNA (Sereti and Altfeld, 2016), fibrosis of lymphoid structure linked to CD4+ T cells depletion (Beignon et al., 2005) and mucosal barriers damages associated with microbial translocation (Klatt and Brenchley, 2010; Gordon et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from Beignon et al., 2005

claim: HIV infection triggers immune activation/dysfunction and inflammation through mucosal barriers damages associated with microbial translocation.
source: HIV infection triggers immune activation/dysfunction and inflammation through several mechanisms such as direct effects of viral proteins on immune cells (Rieckmann et al., 1991; Lee et al., 2003; Simmons et al., 2001), persistent production of type I and II interferons driven by activation of toll-like receptors with HIV-1 RNA (Sereti and Altfeld, 2016), fibrosis of lymphoid structure linked to CD4+ T cells depletion (Beignon et al., 2005) and mucosal barriers damages associated with microbial translocation (Klatt and Brenchley, 2010; Gordon et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from Klatt and Brenchley, 2010; Gordon et al., 2010

claim: Chronic inflammation can promote viral spread and the replenishment of the reservoir by stimulating the migration of CD4+ T cells to sites of viral replication.
source: Although inflammation can contribute to the early control of HIV infection, immune dysfunction and chronic inflammation can in turn promote viral spread and the replenishment of the reservoir by stimulating the migration of CD4+ T cells to sites of viral replication (Klatt and Silvestri, 2012; Hunt et al., 2011), generating new activated target CD4+ T cells (Biancotto et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from Klatt and Silvestri, 2012; Hunt et al., 2011

claim: Chronic inflammation generates new activated target CD4+ T cells.
source: Although inflammation can contribute to the early control of HIV infection, immune dysfunction and chronic inflammation can in turn promote viral spread and the replenishment of the reservoir by stimulating the migration of CD4+ T cells to sites of viral replication (Klatt and Silvestri, 2012; Hunt et al., 2011), generating new activated target CD4+ T cells (Biancotto et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from Biancotto et al., 2008

claim: Chronic inflammation leads to a reduced ability of the immune system to kill infected cells.
source: This further leads to a reduced ability of the immune system to kill infected cells, and an increased cell-surface expression of immune checkpoints which contributes to the survival of infected cells (Hatano et al., 2013; Chomont et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Hatano et al., 2013; Chomont et al., 2009

claim: Chronic inflammation leads to an increased cell-surface expression of immune checkpoints which contributes to the survival of infected cells.
source: This further leads to a reduced ability of the immune system to kill infected cells, and an increased cell-surface expression of immune checkpoints which contributes to the survival of infected cells (Hatano et al., 2013; Chomont et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Hatano et al., 2013; Chomont et al., 2009

claim: Inflammation stimulates latently infected cells to proliferate and produce virus.
source: Furthermore, its stimulates latently infected cells to proliferate but also to produce the virus (Chun et al., 1998; Cameron et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from Chun et al., 1998; Cameron et al., 2010

claim: Targeting chronic inflammation with IL-21 in ART-treated SIV-infected non-human primates could improve disease prognosis by reducing immune activation and the viral reservoir.
source: Micci et al., 2015 established the proof of concept that targeting chronic inflammation with IL-21, a potent immunomodulatory cytokine, in ART-treated SIV-infected non-human primates could improve disease prognosis by reducing immune activation and the viral reservoir.
evidence: Cited from Micci et al., 2015

claim: The viral reservoir is set within few days after infection.
source: To achieve HIV cure, as the viral reservoir is set within few days after infection (Lewis, 2016), early initiation of novel treatment is required to block reservoirs establishment and may protect the immune system (Rutstein et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Lewis, 2016

claim: Early initiation of novel treatment is required to block reservoirs establishment and may protect the immune system.
source: To achieve HIV cure, as the viral reservoir is set within few days after infection (Lewis, 2016), early initiation of novel treatment is required to block reservoirs establishment and may protect the immune system (Rutstein et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Rutstein et al., 2017

claim: Inflammasomes play important roles in innate immunity and inflammation as multiprotein signalling platforms sensing pathogens and danger signals.
source: Inflammasomes plays important roles in innate immunity and inflammation as multiprotein signalling platforms sensing pathogens, danger signals, and regulating cellular functions (Broz and Dixit, 2016).
evidence: Cited from Broz and Dixit, 2016

claim: Active caspase-1 initiates the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18.
source: Subsequently, active caspase-1 initiates the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 and the induction of pyroptosis, an highly inflammatory form of cell death.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about inflammasome function

claim: Active caspase-1 initiates the induction of pyroptosis, a highly inflammatory form of cell death.
source: Subsequently, active caspase-1 initiates the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 and the induction of pyroptosis, an highly inflammatory form of cell death.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about inflammasome function

claim: HIV-1 induces the formation and action of an inflammasome in several cell types and models.
source: HIV-1 was described to induce the formation and action of an inflammasome in several cell types and models (Doitsh et al., 2014; Biancotto et al., 2007; Ahmad et al., 2002; Song et al., 2006; Wiercinska-Drapalo et al., 2004; Granowitz et al., 1995; Pugliese et al., 2002; Ahmad et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2014; Chattergoon et al., 2014; Pontillo et al., 2012; Pontillo et al., 2013; Walsh et al., 2014; Jakobsen et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from multiple studies

claim: Levels of IL-1β and IL-18 were found to be elevated in HIV-1 infected individuals.
source: Levels of IL-1β and IL-18 were found to be elevated in HIV-1 infected individuals (Biancotto et al., 2007; Ahmad et al., 2002; Song et al., 2006) and to induce HIV-1 production (Wiercinska-Drapalo et al., 2004; Granowitz et al., 1995; Pugliese et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from Biancotto et al., 2007; Ahmad et al., 2002; Song et al., 2006

claim: IL-1β and IL-18 induce HIV-1 production.
source: Levels of IL-1β and IL-18 were found to be elevated in HIV-1 infected individuals (Biancotto et al., 2007; Ahmad et al., 2002; Song et al., 2006) and to induce HIV-1 production (Wiercinska-Drapalo et al., 2004; Granowitz et al., 1995; Pugliese et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from Wiercinska-Drapalo et al., 2004; Granowitz et al., 1995; Pugliese et al., 2002

claim: A higher proportion of blood monocytes from HIV-1 infected patients were ASC specks positive, a hallmark of inflammasome activation.
source: Ahmad et al. found that a higher proportion of blood monocytes from HIV-1 infected patients were ASC specks positive, a hallmark of inflammasome activation (Ahmad et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Ahmad et al., 2018

claim: In innate immune cells such as monocytes/macrophages, dendritic cells and microglial cells, HIV-1 infection results in the activation of an inflammasome involving NLRP3.
source: In innate immune cells, such as monocytes/macrophages (Guo et al., 2014; Chattergoon et al., 2014), dendritic cells (Pontillo et al., 2012; Pontillo et al., 2013) and microglial cells (Walsh et al., 2014), HIV-1 infection results in the activation of an inflammasome involving the PRR nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD), leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-containing proteins (NLR) family member 3 (NLRP3).
evidence: Cited from multiple studies on different cell types

claim: In human monocytes/macrophages, HIV-1 triggers the NLRP3 inflammasome through the detection of HIV-1 RNA by TLRs and the activation of the NF-κB pathway.
source: More specifically, in human monocytes/macrophages, HIV-1 triggers the NLRP3 inflammasome through the detection of HIV-1 RNA by TLRs and the activation of the NF-κB pathway (Jakobsen et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Jakobsen et al., 2013

claim: IFI16 is able to sense HIV-1 in macrophages.
source: IFI16 is also able to sense HIV-1 in macrophages, but it is unknown whether it can activate an inflammasome in such cell type (Jakobsen et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Jakobsen et al., 2013

claim: Over 95% of CD4 T cells are non-permissive to HIV-1 infection and accumulate incomplete DNA transcripts in their cytosol.
source: Over 95% of CD4 T cells are non-permissive to HIV-1 infection and accumulates incomplete DNA transcripts in their cytosol.
evidence: Based on findings from Doitsh et al., 2010 using lymphoid aggregate culture systems

claim: Incomplete HIV-1 DNA transcripts in CD4+ T cells are detected by IFI16, which activates caspase-1, triggers pyroptosis and the release of intracellular content and pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1β.
source: These transcripts are detected by IFI16, a sensor which activates caspase-1, triggers pyroptosis and the release of intracellular content and pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1β (Monroe et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Monroe et al., 2014

claim: The role of the inflammasome in early SIV pathogenesis has been shown in the impairment of the innate and adaptive immune response.
source: The role of the inflammasome in early SIV pathogenesis has recently been shown in the impairment of the innate and adaptive immune response (Barouch et al., 2016) thereby facilitating viral replication (Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from Barouch et al., 2016

claim: Inflammasome activation facilitates viral replication in SIV infection.
source: The role of the inflammasome in early SIV pathogenesis has recently been shown in the impairment of the innate and adaptive immune response (Barouch et al., 2016) thereby facilitating viral replication (Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from Lu et al., 2016

claim: VX-765 is a selective caspase 1 inhibitor that reduces activation and activity of caspase 1 and antagonizes NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and activation.
source: VX-765, a selective caspase 1 inhibitor, reduces activation and activity of caspase 1 and antagonizes NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and activation in the context of several inflammatory disorders and diseases such as atherosclerosis, sepsis, or alzheimer disease (Jin et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2021; Flores et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Jin et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2021; Flores et al., 2020

claim: Humanized mice recapitulate key aspects of HIV-1 infection and pathogenesis.
source: Humanized mice recapitulate key aspects of HIV-1 infection and pathogenesis (Singh et al., 2012; Adams et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Singh et al., 2012; Adams et al., 2021

claim: Viremia was detectable in 60% of animals sacrificed on day 10 post-infection and 100% of animals sacrificed on day 24 post-infection.
source: Viremia was detectable in 3 (60%) and 5 (100%) animals sacrificed on day 10 and 24 post-infection (p.i.), respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Acute HIV-1 infection in huNSG mice was associated with a profound decrease in CD4+ T cell percentages in the blood at day 24 when compared to animals sacrificed at day 10 post-infection.
source: Acute HIV-1 infection in huNSG mice was associated with a profound decrease in CD4+ T cell percentages in the blood at day 24 when compared to animals sacrificed at day 10 post-infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental data from the study shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: All huNSG mice necropsied at day 1 following HIV-1JRCSF challenge were negative for viral RNA.
source: All huNSG mice necropsied at day 1 following HIV-1JRCSF challenge were negative for viral RNA, whereas huNSG mice sacrificed at day 3 displayed at least one tissue positive for viral RNA with the spleen and the lung being positive in 80% (4 of 5) and 60% (3 of 5) animals, respectively, indicating viral dissemination at least within 72 hr.
evidence: Experimental data from RT-PCR measurements in tissues

claim: HuNSG mice sacrificed at day 3 displayed at least one tissue positive for viral RNA with the spleen and the lung being positive in 80% and 60% of animals, respectively, indicating viral dissemination within 72 hr.
source: All huNSG mice necropsied at day 1 following HIV-1JRCSF challenge were negative for viral RNA, whereas huNSG mice sacrificed at day 3 displayed at least one tissue positive for viral RNA with the spleen and the lung being positive in 80% (4 of 5) and 60% (3 of 5) animals, respectively, indicating viral dissemination at least within 72 hr.
evidence: Experimental data from RT-PCR measurements in tissues, with inference about viral dissemination

claim: Tissue viral RNA levels became detectable in the lymph nodes (5 of 5) and the blood (4 of 5) in animals sacrificed on day 10 post-infection.
source: Tissue viral RNA levels became detectable in the lymph nodes (5 of 5) and the blood (4 of 5) in animal sacrificed on day 10 p.i.
evidence: Experimental data from RT-PCR measurements

claim: A bi-phasic induction of inflammasome related-genes upon HIV-1 infection was observed in the bone marrow, lymph nodes, and spleen.
source: We observed a bi-phasic induction of inflammasome related-genes upon HIV-1 infection in the bone marrow, lymph nodes, and spleen (Figure 1).
evidence: Experimental data from gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1

claim: In the bone marrow, a striking but short-lasting early upregulation of inflammasome components appeared around 3 days post-infection, including NLRP3 (p<0.05), ASC (p<0.01), CASP-1 (p<0.01), IL-1β (p<0.01), and IL-18 (p<0.01).
source: In the bone marrow, a striking but short-lasting early upregulation of inflammasome components appeared around 3 days p.i. These included the NOD-like receptor NLRP3 (p<0.05), the adaptor ASC (p<0.01), bridging NLRs such as NLRP3 to the inflammatory Caspase-1 (CASP-1) (p<0.01) and the downstream pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β (p<0.01)and IL-18 (p<0.01)indicating the up-regulation of the whole NLRP3 pathway.
evidence: Experimental data from gene expression analysis in bone marrow

claim: In the lymph nodes, the induction of an early inflammasome response was evident as soon as day 1 and 3 post-infection with the upregulation of NLRP1 (p<0.05), NLRP3 (p<0.01), AIM2 (p<0.05), CASP-1 (p<0.01) and IL-1b (p<0.01).
source: In the lymph nodes, the induction of an early inflammasome response was evident as soon as day 1 and 3 p.i. with the upregulation of the NOD-like receptors NLRP1 (p<0.05) and NLRP3 (p<0.01), AIM2 (p<0.05), CASP-1 (p<0.01) and IL-1b (p<0.01).
evidence: Experimental data from gene expression analysis in lymph nodes

claim: In the lymph nodes, the initial burst of inflammasome gene expression was sustained with prolonged upregulation of NLRP3, AIM2, and CASP1 (p≤0.05) up to day 24 post-infection.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to the bone marrow, this initial burst was sustained in the lymph nodes with the prolonged upregulation of several genes (p≤0.05 for NLRP3, AIM2, and CASP1) up to day 24 p.i.
evidence: Experimental data from gene expression analysis in lymph nodes

claim: In the spleen, AIM2 was the only significantly upregulated gene at 3 days post-infection (p<0.05).
source: In the spleen, AIM2 was the only significantly upregulated gene at 3 days p.i. (p<0.05), although we observed a tendency for other genes (NLRP3, NLRC4, CASP1, and IL1Β) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Experimental data from gene expression analysis in spleen shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Rapid inflammasome-related transcriptomic changes indicate an early sensing of HIV-1 infection, especially in the bone marrow and lymph nodes, before HIV-1 RNA was quantifiable in tissues.
source: Altogether, these rapid inflammasome-related transcriptomic changes indicate an early sensing of HIV-1 infection, especially in the bone marrow and lymph nodes, before HIV-1 RNA was quantifiable in tissues (Figure 1) and may reflect the host response to the inoculum challenge virus.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data comparing gene expression timing with viral RNA detection

claim: IFI16 restricts HIV-1 infection in macrophages.
source: Importantly, IFI16 restricts HIV-1 infection in macrophages but promotes HIV-1 induced CD4+ T cells death by pyroptosis and thus may drive HIV-1 pathogenesis (Doitsh et al., 2010; Monroe et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Doitsh et al., 2010; Monroe et al., 2014

claim: IFI16 promotes HIV-1 induced CD4+ T cells death by pyroptosis and thus may drive HIV-1 pathogenesis.
source: Importantly, IFI16 restricts HIV-1 infection in macrophages but promotes HIV-1 induced CD4+ T cells death by pyroptosis and thus may drive HIV-1 pathogenesis (Doitsh et al., 2010; Monroe et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Doitsh et al., 2010; Monroe et al., 2014

claim: IFI16 upregulation was common in all three organs (bone marrow, lymph nodes, spleen), with maximal transcription at 24 days post-infection (p<0.01, 0.05 and 0.01 respectively).
source: Interestingly, in our humanized mice model, the upregulation of IFI16 was common in all three organs, with a maximal transcription at 24 days p.i. (p<0.01, 0.05 and 0.01 in bone marrow, lymph nodes, and spleen, respectively) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Experimental data from gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: IFI16 expression was higher in viremic mice and correlated with corresponding tissue viral RNA copies (p=0.0007 in bone marrow and p=0.005 in the spleen).
source: Furthermore, IFI16 expression was higher in viremic mice (Figure 2A) and correlated with corresponding tissue viral RNA copies (Figure 2B; p=0.0007 in bone marrow and p=0.005 in the spleen) and with CD4+ T cells percentage in the blood (Figure 2C; p=0.0019 for the spleen).
evidence: Experimental data showing correlation analysis in Figure 2

claim: IFI16 expression correlated with CD4+ T cells percentage in the blood (p=0.0019 for the spleen).
source: Furthermore, IFI16 expression was higher in viremic mice (Figure 2A) and correlated with corresponding tissue viral RNA copies (Figure 2B; p=0.0007 in bone marrow and p=0.005 in the spleen) and with CD4+ T cells percentage in the blood (Figure 2C; p=0.0019 for the spleen).
evidence: Experimental data showing correlation analysis in Figure 2

claim: AIM2 reached a maximum of expression at day 24 post-infection in the bone marrow, lymph nodes and the spleen (p<0.05, p<0.005 and p<0.005, respectively).
source: Similarly, AIM2 reached a maximum of expression at day 24 p.i. in the bone marrow, lymph nodes and the spleen (p<0.05, p<0.005 and p<0.005, respectively) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Experimental data from gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: AIM2 was expressed at higher levels in viremic mice when compared to non-viremic mice (p<0.001 and 0.05 in lymph nodes and spleen, respectively).
source: Similarly, AIM2 reached a maximum of expression at day 24 p.i. in the bone marrow, lymph nodes and the spleen (p<0.05, p<0.005 and p<0.005, respectively) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and was expressed at higher levels in viremic mice when compared to non-viremic mice (p<0.001 and 0.05 in lymph nodes and spleen, respectively) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Experimental data comparing AIM2 expression between viremic and non-viremic mice shown in Figure 2D

claim: AIM2 expression correlated with viral RNA copies in the same organ (p<0.05 in lymph nodes and spleen).
source: AIM2 expression also correlated with viral RNA copies in the same organ (Figure 2E; p<0.05 in lymph nodes and spleen) and inversely with CD4+ T cells percentage in the blood (Figure 2F; p<0.05 in the spleen).
evidence: Experimental data showing correlation analysis in Figure 2E

claim: AIM2 expression inversely correlated with CD4+ T cells percentage in the blood (p<0.05 in the spleen).
source: AIM2 expression also correlated with viral RNA copies in the same organ (Figure 2E; p<0.05 in lymph nodes and spleen) and inversely with CD4+ T cells percentage in the blood (Figure 2F; p<0.05 in the spleen).
evidence: Experimental data showing correlation analysis in Figure 2F

claim: ASC and CASP1 reached a maximum of expression 24 days post-infection, notably in the spleen (p<0.01 for both) and in the lymph nodes (p<0.01 for CASP1).
source: In addition, other inflammasome-related genes (ASC and CASP1) reached a maximum of expression 24 days p.i., notably in the spleen (p<0.01; ASC, CASP1) and in the lymph nodes (p<0.01; CASP1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Experimental data from gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: ASC expression was associated with HIV-1 replication in the bone marrow (p<0.05) and HIV-1 pathogenesis in the bone marrow and the spleen (p<0.05).
source: In addition, other inflammasome-related genes (ASC and CASP1) reached a maximum of expression 24 days p.i., notably in the spleen (p<0.01; ASC, CASP1) and in the lymph nodes (p<0.01; CASP1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and their expression was associated with HIV-1 replication in the bone marrow for ASC (p<0.05) and HIV-1 pathogenesis for ASC in the bone marrow and the spleen (p<0.05) and for CASP-1 in the lymph nodes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, p<0.05).

claim: CASP-1 expression was associated with HIV-1 pathogenesis in the lymph nodes (p<0.05).
